We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.
record.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning

record.abstract: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.
record.title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers

record.abstract: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.
record.title: Distill the Correction, Not the Rewrite: Hindsight Twins for Self-Improving Text-to-Image Models

record.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
record.comments: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/
record.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware

record.abstract: Most LLM agent frameworks build a crew that runs a task and exits. Physical environments (e.g., homes, labs, factory floors) need agents that stay up for months, survive their own bugs, and run on whatever hardware is already next to the sensors. We present Wactorz, an open-source runtime in which LLM-generated agents are long-lived, supervised actors: a planner turns a chat request into Python, compiles it into a new actor at runtime, and a supervisor restarts that actor alone, with its state intact, when it crashes. All coordination rides on MQTT, so agents can be spawned on, and live-migrated between, edge nodes such as a Raspberry Pi, and every internal event is a topic external systems can subscribe to. The recorded demo builds a camera-to-lamp automation from one chat request, adds a second agent that is auto-wired to the first by topic and carries a deliberate division-by-zero, watches that agent repair its own code without losing its count, then deploys a fresh Raspberry Pi node and live-migrates the agent onto it, in under four minutes of wall-clock time and \$0.13 of model usage. This extended version adds what the two-page demonstration paper could not: the Wiring view of the topic graph, Wactorz as a library for hand-written agents, how trained models are stored, sent to nodes and replaced, the security model, and the system's limitations.
record.comments: 5 pages. 2 figues. Extended version of a paper accepted to the AAAI-27 Demonstrations Program. Code: https://github.com/waldiez/wactorz
record.title: Wactorz: Self-Writing LLM Agents That Discover, Repair, and Migrate at the Edge

record.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
record.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research

record.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
record.title: Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation

record.abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
record.title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields

record.abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.
record.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events

record.abstract: For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine's coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player's interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player's own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.
record.title: GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models

record.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
record.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models

record.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
record.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations

We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.
record.title: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence

record.abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
record.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark

record.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.
record.comments: 10 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zwang-devv/intent-contracts
record.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents

record.abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.
record.title: Autoregressive View Model

record.abstract: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wrocław, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. With the query's photographer withheld, learned local-feature matching raises DINOv2 accuracy from 81.8% to 85.5% and also improves DINOv3. Comparing the two best candidates cuts DINOv2's false acceptance of unknown statues from 38.3% to 19.6% at 90% known acceptance.
record.comments: 23 pages, 6 figures in the main text; includes appendix. Project page: https://turhancan97.github.io/doppeldwarf-306/
record.title: Which Dwarf Is This? Doppeldwarf-306 and Near-Identical Instance Retrieval

record.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.
record.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing

Microsoft、PowerPointは、マイクロソフト グループの企業の商標です。 Sakana AI Sakana AIは、AIの未来を私たちと一緒に切り拓いてくださる方を募集しています。当社の 募集要項 をご覧ください。 English Announcement Sakana Marlin Update: Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0, Two New Modes for Faster and Deeper Research, plus Redesigned Slides Today Sakana AI is updating Sakana Marlin with two new research modes, Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0, that raise the depth, speed and breadth of its research. We have also substantially improved the quality of the slides it exports in Microsoft PowerPoint format. Twilight 2.0: More angles, in less time Midnight 2.0: The widest view, for new discoveries The Sakana Marlin you have been using remains available as Sunlight, a lighter mode. The ocean changes with depth. The shallow layer that sunlight reaches is called the sunlight zone, the layer where only faint light arrives is the twilight zone, and the deep layer that no light reaches at all is the midnight zone. Research is similar: some information can be found near the surface, and some structures only come into view when you dive deep. The three modes take their names from these layers of the sea. The layers of the sea that give the three modes their names The Idea Behind Sakana Marlin When we launched Sakana Marlin in June, we described it in a single line: leave the research to AI, so people can focus on the decision making. Sakana Marlin is a strategic research agent. Give it a topic, and it works autonomously from framing hypotheses through gathering and testing evidence to writing up the findings as a report, in support of people facing big decisions in uncertain times. Since launch, it has been used for strategy work, market and competitor analysis, regulatory research and much else. In September we added Interactive Reading, which lets you move between a report and its sources while talking with the AI, and PowerPoint slide export. With them we have been strengthening the experience of understanding the findings deeply, confirming them and turning them into action. Answering the Call for Both Depth and Speed As more people came to rely on Sakana Marlin, we heard more and more requests for a higher standard of depth, speed and breadth: “Before a meeting, I want to grasp the big picture quickly.” “In a field I know well, I want analysis that goes further, and more angles on the question.” From a first overview to a deep dive in a specialist field, which of these matters most depends on the purpose and the stage of the research. AI technology has been moving quickly too. Over the past few months, inference-time scaling, in which a system spends more compute at inference time to raise the quality of its output, has been moving into the mainstream of AI development. Sakana Marlin has been built on this idea from the start. Technical details are available in our beta-release blog post . But as we wrote then, results do not improve in proportion to the compute put in. In real-world research, where no single right answer exists, it is hard to say what makes research good in the first place: evaluating quality is itself the difficult part. Without a settled way to judge the output, piling on more inference does not produce stable quality. Thinking longer is not the same as thinking better. 1. New Modes, Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0: Faster, Deeper and Broader Research For this update we brought together two bodies of know-how: what we have learned about inference-time scaling, and what we have learned about evaluating the output of AI on complex, demanding intellectual work in the real world. The result is two new modes that spend even more inference than before and reach a depth and breadth that offer new insight even to experts in the field. As the research proceeds, the new modes reframe their own questions in light of what they find, and keep digging while updating their hypotheses. Rather than jumping to a single conclusion, they keep testing it: is that really so, and is there another possibility? We have built that attitude, the question of what makes research good, into the research process itself. With Sunlight alongside them, Sakana Marlin now lets you choose, from three modes, the speed and depth that suit the task. Twilight 2.0: captures the overall picture and structure of a topic quickly and broadly. It comes into its own when you need to get the issues straight before your next meeting, or to survey an unfamiliar field quickly ahead of a new project. Midnight 2.0: combines comprehensive coverage of the issues with deep exploration and rigorous verification. It is the best fit when you want to draw fresh insight from a field you already know, or when the work calls for thorough substantiation and specialist depth. Sunlight: the Sakana Marlin you know. It remains available for general use where you want to complete research at lower cost. A run uses 100 credits in Sunlight and 300 in Twilight 2.0 or Midnight 2.0. Twilight 2.0 finishes more than an hour sooner than Sunlight while drawing on about three times as many sources. Midnight 2.0 draws on about seven times as many sources, and its reports are about five times as long. Processing time, report length and sources cited in the three modes To use a new mode, simply choose it when you request research. Choose a mode when you request research 2. Redesigned Slides: The Key Points of a Long Report, in the Slides Alone The second update is a redesign of PowerPoint slide export. The new slides are available in all three modes: Sunlight, Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0. In Twilight 2.0 and Midnight 2.0 the research goes deeper, and the reports have grown longer with it. When there is no time to read the full text, or when you present the findings in a meeting, slides that pull the key points together matter more than ever. So we strengthened slide generation so that the slides alone are enough to grasp the outline of the research. We developed a new dedicated harness for an AI agent to build slides, and built into it the know-how needed to make slides at a professional level. Working from that know-how, the agent reads the whole report, designs the storyline, assembles the slides, then checks the rendered result itself and fixes it. The deck opens with a cover, a table of contents and an executive summary, and tells the whole report as a single story. Each slide states its message in a single headline sentence, draws the structure of the issues and their causal links as diagrams, shows quantitative data as charts, and carries source URLs. Slide templates are still supported, so the same content can be produced in your company’s template or one specified by a client. Example of the new output slides However deep the research goes, it does not lead to a decision unless it gets across. Researching deeply, and conveying briefly: the new slides are there to deliver both from a single run. See the Sample Reports for Yourself The best way to see how the output has changed with the new modes is to look at an actual report. On the product page you can view and download sample reports and slides created by Sakana Marlin. See the sample reports： https://sakana.ai/marlin/#usecase Sakana AI’s products will continue working toward a world where people and AI are attuned to each other and better decisions follow. Nanoのベースモデル（事前学習モデル）に対して、継続事前学習から事後学習までを自社で行った、300億パラメータの大規模言語モデル（LLM）です。 Sakana Namazu で培った事後学習技術に加えて、今回新たに開発した継続事前学習ならびに事後学習技術を、手元の環境で動かせるサイズのモデルに適用しました。Sakana Namazuは、オープンモデルを土台に私たちの事後学習技術で仕上げたモデルの名称で、Sakana Namazu Smallはその系譜に連なる小型のモデルです。日常的な対話、Web検索を用いた調査、長い文書の読解など、日常的な業務を得意としています。 Sakana Namazu model）として開発しています。複雑な質問やタスクに対しても、必要な情報を整理し、推論を重ねながら回答を導き出すことを目指しています。 ユースケース Sakana Namazu Smallは、日常的な対話に加え、特に次のような業務での活用を想定しています。 長い文書を読み、根拠を示して答える仕事： 社内文書や報告書を読み込んで質問に答える、複数の資料から必要な情報を整理する、出典を明示しながら要約するといった用途です。長文の読解や、与えられた資料に忠実に回答する能力を生かし、文書を活用した業務を支援します。 Web検索を組み合わせた調査： 最新のニュースや業界動向の調査、複数の情報源を横断した情報収集などの用途です。単純な検索では答えが見つからない質問に対しても、Web検索を繰り返しながら情報を収集・整理し、回答を導き出すことを得意としています。 Sakana AIの最近のニュースについての質問に対するSakana Namazu Smallによる回答例の一部。 ベンチマーク結果 Sakana Namazu Smallの性能を検証するため、同規模のNVIDIA Nemotron™ 3 Nano（30B-A3B）と、総パラメータ数が約4倍のNVIDIA Nemotron™ 3 Super（120B-A12B）と性能比較を行いました。比較対象のNemotronモデルには、いずれもNVIDIA®社が事後学習まで行ったモデルを使用しています。 評価には、Web検索を活用した調査能力、指示追従能力、長文理解・根拠に基づく回答能力、一般知識や専門知識などを測る、合計25種類のベンチマークを使用しました。例えば、Web検索用の性能評価にはBrowseComp 1 やFRAMES 2 、長文理解にはLLM-jp LongBench 3 やLongBench v2 4 、一般知識や専門知識理解にはSimpleQA Verified 5 特に高い性能を示したのが、Web検索を活用した調査と、長い文書を理解して根拠に基づき回答するタスクです。一方で、Web検索等の外部情報に頼らずモデルの内部知識のみで回答するタスク（Knowledge）では、性能が大きく伸びていません。今後は、こうした強みをさらに伸ばすとともに、知識に関する能力の改善にも取り組んでいきます。 今後の展開 Sakana Namazu Sakana Namazu Small, a 30-billion-parameter large language model (LLM) built on the pretrained base model of NVIDIA® Nemotron™ 3 Nano, an open model from NVIDIA. We handled everything in-house, from continued pretraining through post-training. On top of the post-training techniques we developed for Sakana Namazu , we built new continued pretraining and post-training techniques for this release and applied them to a model small enough to run in your own environment. Sakana Namazu is the name we give to models built on open models and finished with our post-training techniques, and Sakana Namazu Small is a compact member of that family. It is good at day-to-day work such as everyday conversation, research with web search, and reading long documents. Because Sakana Namazu Small is small enough to run in your own environment, we also plan to offer it on-premises. We plan to share details on on-premises availability in early-to-mid December. Key features of Sakana Namazu Small Pretraining alone does not determine a model’s performance. Continued pretraining and post-training are where we shape the capabilities a given use case needs, such as agentic and conversational abilities. For this release, we focused on the capabilities that real work calls for, such as everyday conversation, gathering information with web search, and understanding long documents and answering from evidence. We also developed Sakana Namazu Small as a reasoning model. Even for complex questions and tasks, it is designed to organize the information it needs and reason step by step toward an answer. Use cases Beyond everyday conversation, we expect Sakana Namazu Small to be especially useful for the following kinds of work. Reading long documents and answering with evidence: Answering questions over internal documents and reports, pulling together the information you need from multiple sources, and summarizing with citations. The model’s ability to read long texts and stay faithful to the material it is given supports document-based work. Research with web search: Researching the latest news and industry trends, or gathering information across multiple sources. Even when a simple search won’t surface the answer, the model is good at searching repeatedly, collecting and organizing what it finds, and working out an answer. Part of a response from Sakana Namazu Small to a question about recent Sakana AI news. Benchmark results We compared Sakana Namazu Small against NVIDIA® Nemotron™ 3 Nano (30B-A3B), which is the same size, and NVIDIA® Nemotron™ 3 Super (120B-A12B), which is roughly four times larger. For both Nemotron models, we used the versions post-trained by NVIDIA. For the evaluation, we used 25 benchmarks in total, measuring research with web search, instruction following, long-document understanding and evidence-based answering, and general and specialized knowledge. For example, we used BrowseComp 1 and FRAMES 2 for web search, LLM-jp LongBench 3 and LongBench v2 4 for long-document understanding, and SimpleQA Verified 5 and MedRECT 6 for general and specialized knowledge. As a result, Sakana Namazu Small outperformed not only Nemotron 3 Nano, which is the same size, but also Nemotron 3 Super, which is roughly four times larger, on the average score across the 25 benchmarks. Average score across 25 benchmarks measuring web search, long-document reading, and knowledge accuracy, and average scores by task type. The model performed especially well on research with web search and on tasks that require understanding long documents and answering from evidence. On tasks answered from the model’s internal knowledge alone, without external information such as web search, performance did not improve much. We will keep building on these strengths while working to improve the model’s knowledge. What’s next We will keep improving Sakana Namazu Small, and we plan to apply what we learn to our next generation of models and products. At 30 billion parameters, the model is a size that companies can consider running on their own infrastructure. We plan to share details on on-premises availability for Sakana Namazu Small in early-to-mid December 2026. We want to achieve high performance with limited compute, so that more people can use AI in their own environments. Sakana Namazu Small is one of our efforts to put that idea into practice. We are looking for people to join us in building models like this in Japan and delivering them to people around the world. If you’re interested, see our careers page . This model builds on results from research and development supported by GENIAC (Generative AI Accelerator Challenge), a project run by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and NEDO to strengthen domestic generative AI development and accelerate its adoption in society. record.abstract: We present BrowseComp, a simple yet challenging benchmark for measuring the ability for agents to browse the web. BrowseComp comprises 1,266 questions that require persistently navigating the internet in search of hard-to-find, entangled information. Despite the difficulty of the questions, BrowseComp is simple and easy-to-use, as predicted answers are short and easily verifiable against reference answers. BrowseComp for browsing agents can be seen as analogous to how programming competitions are an incomplete but useful benchmark for coding agents. While BrowseComp sidesteps challenges of a true user query distribution, like generating long answers or resolving ambiguity, it measures the important core capability of exercising persistence and creativity in finding information. BrowseComp can be found at https://github.com/openai/simple-evals.
record.title: BrowseComp: A Simple Yet Challenging Benchmark for Browsing Agents

record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant performance improvements across various cognitive tasks. An emerging application is using LLMs to enhance retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) capabilities. These systems require LLMs to understand user queries, retrieve relevant information, and synthesize coherent and accurate responses. Given the increasing real-world deployment of such systems, comprehensive evaluation becomes crucial. To this end, we propose FRAMES (Factuality, Retrieval, And reasoning MEasurement Set), a high-quality evaluation dataset designed to test LLMs' ability to provide factual responses, assess retrieval capabilities, and evaluate the reasoning required to generate final answers. While previous work has provided datasets and benchmarks to evaluate these abilities in isolation, FRAMES offers a unified framework that provides a clearer picture of LLM performance in end-to-end RAG scenarios. Our dataset comprises challenging multi-hop questions that require the integration of information from multiple sources. We present baseline results demonstrating that even state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with this task, achieving 0.40 accuracy with no retrieval. The accuracy is significantly improved with our proposed multi-step retrieval pipeline, achieving an accuracy of 0.66 (>50% improvement). We hope our work will help bridge evaluation gaps and assist in developing more robust and capable RAG systems.
record.comments: Annual Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL), 2025
record.title: Fact, Fetch, and Reason: A Unified Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation

record.abstract: This paper introduces LongBench v2, a benchmark designed to assess the ability of LLMs to handle long-context problems requiring deep understanding and reasoning across real-world multitasks. LongBench v2 consists of 503 challenging multiple-choice questions, with contexts ranging from 8k to 2M words, across six major task categories: single-document QA, multi-document QA, long in-context learning, long-dialogue history understanding, code repository understanding, and long structured data understanding. To ensure the breadth and the practicality, we collect data from nearly 100 highly educated individuals with diverse professional backgrounds. We employ both automated and manual review processes to maintain high quality and difficulty, resulting in human experts achieving only 53.7% accuracy under a 15-minute time constraint. Our evaluation reveals that the best-performing model, when directly answers the questions, achieves only 50.1% accuracy. In contrast, the o1-preview model, which includes longer reasoning, achieves 57.7%, surpassing the human baseline by 4%. These results highlight the importance of enhanced reasoning ability and scaling inference-time compute to tackle the long-context challenges in LongBench v2. The project is available at https://longbench2.github.io.
record.title: LongBench v2: Towards Deeper Understanding and Reasoning on Realistic Long-context Multitasks

record.abstract: We introduce SimpleQA Verified, a 1,000-prompt benchmark for evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) short-form factuality based on OpenAI's SimpleQA. It addresses critical limitations in OpenAI's benchmark, including noisy and incorrect labels, topical biases, and question redundancy. SimpleQA Verified was created through a rigorous multi-stage filtering process involving de-duplication, topic balancing, and source reconciliation to produce a more reliable and challenging evaluation set, alongside improvements in the autorater prompt. On this new benchmark, Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves a state-of-the-art F1-score of 55.6, outperforming other frontier models, including GPT-5. This work provides the research community with a higher-fidelity tool to track genuine progress in parametric model factuality and to mitigate hallucinations. The benchmark dataset, evaluation code, and leaderboard are available at: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/deepmind/simpleqa-verified.
record.title: SimpleQA Verified: A Reliable Factuality Benchmark to Measure Parametric Knowledge

record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in medical applications, but their ability to detect and correct errors in clinical texts remains under-evaluated, particularly beyond English. We introduce MedRECT, a bilingual benchmark for Japanese and English that formulates medical error handling as three subtasks: error detection, error sentence extraction, and error correction. MedRECT-ja contains 663 samples derived from the Japanese Medical Licensing Examinations, while the separately sourced MedRECT-en contains 458 samples curated from MEDEC. We evaluate 11 LLMs across 17 configurations that cover proprietary and open-weight models, medical-domain specialization, and multiple reasoning settings. Qwen3-32B scores higher in its thinking mode than in its non-thinking mode on error detection F1 and sentence extraction accuracy in both subsets, with sentence extraction accuracy higher by 24.5 percentage points on MedRECT-ja and 10.3 on MedRECT-en. Several leading general-purpose reasoning models outperform all three evaluated medical-domain models on these two subtasks. Most models have lower point estimates on the Japanese subset, although absolute scores are not directly comparable because the subsets differ in source material and error distributions. LoRA fine-tuning yields higher sentence extraction accuracy and higher point estimates on all three reference-based correction similarity metrics in both languages. MedRECT provides an open, reusable evaluation resource for studying medical error correction and reasoning across Japanese and English. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/pfnet-research/medrect.
record.comments: 16 pages. To appear at the EMNLP 2026 Workshop on Open Reasoning Across Cultures & Languages (ORACLE)
record.title: MedRECT: A Bilingual Medical Reasoning Benchmark for Error Correction in Clinical Texts

record.abstract: OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models it has trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from its own codebase. It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025. If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it. Under standard scaling laws , each tenfold increase in compute buys a smaller drop in loss than the last, so naively we would expect progress in loss to slow down over time (see figure below). 1 Among METR staff there remains active discussion on how to interpret this dramatic acceleration in pretraining progress, and how to reconcile it with the lack of a comparable acceleration in benchmark scores of OpenAI’s models, e.g. as reflected in Epoch’s ECI . Concretely, it remains arguable how much this new information should change our forecasts of future AI capabilities. The following considerations are important: It is possible that the data released overstates true progress in pretraining, e.g. through various types of overfitting. More data would help substantially here. It is possible that benchmark scores are the best measure of real-world capabilities, and pretraining perplexity is only informative as an input. This implies the new data showing acceleration in pretraining progress would not substantially change our forecasts of future capabilities. 2 However, to the extent that AI contributed to the acceleration in pretraining, this gives us a sign of AI’s likely future contribution to all parts of the model-training pipeline. 3 It is possible that pretraining perplexity reflects a fundamentally deeper measure of model capability than the typical benchmarks used to evaluate models. Many AI researchers treat pretraining perplexity in this way, and expect that OpenAI’s rapid acceleration in pretraining will be followed by an acceleration in capabilities measured by real-world impact. 4 There remain substantial disagreements on how much this information should modify our projections of the future path of capabilities, and METR does not have a consensus view on this. Some interpretations imply that OpenAI’s data on acceleration in pretraining should make us expect a broad-based acceleration in real-world AI capabilities over the next six months. To our knowledge, no frontier developer had previously published how the pretraining loss of its successive frontier models has changed over multiple years on a fixed held-out dataset. This information is typically considered highly commercially sensitive. However, we think publishing information about pretraining loss is very valuable for informing the public about the prospect of AI R&D acceleration. We encourage all AI developers to do the same, as Microsoft has since done for its own models using OpenAI’s dataset, and to share additional context that would let external researchers better understand the degree of acceleration, what’s driving it, and whether we should expect it to continue and/or compound. 5 The following would be especially informative: Log-perplexity on other held-out datasets. Loss measured on a single corpus may not capture progress on other kinds of text. OpenAI’s plot, for example, reports loss on a corpus sourced from its own internal codebase. Recent recipes or data could help on that kind of text (e.g. coding) more than on others, or small parts of the codebase could have leaked into training data. Log-perplexity on other very different held-out datasets (e.g. a corpus of books) would be informative about the robustness of this trend. 6 Eventually, these held-out corpora could be maintained by a third party, making it possible to compare trends in pretraining loss across AI developers. The rough date that the pretraining run ended for each model. Plotting models at their public release dates may not capture when pretraining progress happened: log-perplexity is a property of the base model, and base models could be finished months before release. If the lag between the end of the pretraining run and model release shrank over time, the acceleration in loss would be smaller than the plot suggests (and vice versa). More importantly, knowing the lag helps us determine how much AI uplift contributed to the pretraining gains: regardless of when a model was released, we can’t attribute its pretraining gains to AI agents if its pretraining happened when researchers barely used AI agents. How pretraining compute, labor spending, and experiment compute changed over time. Lower pretraining loss could be attributable to a number of factors: for example, increased training compute, increased labor or experimental compute spending, or increased uplift from AI assistance. Some of these factors imply that we should expect the growth to be a one-time spike, while others imply that we should expect it to continue; if it is substantially attributable to AI uplift, the acceleration could compound. To understand this, it would be helpful to have a sense of how these resources were growing in the relevant time period. One way to see this is to convert log-perplexity into “effective compute”: the compute that a single fixed recipe would need to reach a given loss value. If we assumed that all of OpenAI’s models are on the same scaling law with irreducible loss between 0.3 and 0.6, effective compute would have grown roughly 8 to 10 times faster since early 2026 than in 2022–2025, measured in orders of magnitude per year. However, that assumption is unrealistic, since newer recipes likely follow different scaling laws. ↩︎ For example, architectural changes that spend more computation per token, such as looped transformers, might lower perplexity more than they improve downstream capabilities, since standard models could reach similar capabilities after post-training by reasoning in a chain of thought. ↩︎ A footnote in OpenAI’s post is consistent with AI playing a small role at the start of the acceleration, but a larger role currently: “We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.” Similarly, METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic found that the acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors, but estimated that “a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.” ↩︎ A related argument why this data on pretraining acceleration should modify our forecasts of real-world capabilities is that our scales of capability, such as ECI, MCI , and time horizon, are sensitive to delicate statistical assumptions, or rely heavily on a few benchmarks that are close to saturation. ↩︎ Many other kinds of information would also help, but we have focused on a few numbers that we expect companies already collect and should be relatively simple to share. ↩︎ The other held-out datasets should date from before 2022, so that they don’t contain any AI-generated text. Ideally, they would cover a variety of text types, such as code, scientific writing, and prose, to show how much of the trend on the original held-out set reflects progress on code specifically. ↩︎
record.title: Interpreting a recent acceleration in pretraining loss

record.abstract: We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a transformer language model under a given compute budget. We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled. We test this hypothesis by training a predicted compute-optimal model, Chinchilla, that uses the same compute budget as Gopher but with 70B parameters and 4$\times$ more more data. Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks. This also means that Chinchilla uses substantially less compute for fine-tuning and inference, greatly facilitating downstream usage. As a highlight, Chinchilla reaches a state-of-the-art average accuracy of 67.5% on the MMLU benchmark, greater than a 7% improvement over Gopher.

title.before: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
title.official: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?

abstract.before: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

title.official: From Token Bills to Benchmark Weeks: Making Auto-Research for Data Systems Verifiable and Affordable

abstract.before: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.
abstract.official: Scientific predictors guide costly experiments, yet returned measurements often reveal errors that matter for subsequent experimental choices. WeightLoop turns this feedback into persistent model updates through a reusable Weight-Space Programming (WSP) editor. We use GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek to construct update programs from the scientific objective, model computation and editable parameters. These programs use accumulated measurements to estimate parameter corrections, validate them on feedback and save accepted changes in the original model. With identical feedback and writable parameters, four pretrained scientific predictors obtain 5.10-18.56% lower primary error. For weather prediction, changing four output-bias parameters reduces root mean squared error by 13.28%. Functional ranking and sequential discovery further connect reusable editing programs to improved experimental choices.

abstract.before: Robot agents built on vision-language models depend on both the planner and its harness: the tools, feedback, memory, and recovery logic around it. Can improvements to a large teacher's harness be carried into a compact agent with lower inference compute cost? We present TinyAstral, a two-stage approach. We first freeze an open-weight teacher and improve its harness through recursive self-improvement (RSI): frontier LLM agents read the teacher's trajectories and propose harness edits, and each edit is accepted only if it passes a paired statistical test. We then freeze the final harness, collect teacher trajectories with reasoning and failure recovery, and distill a small student that replaces the teacher in the same harness. On RoboTwin, harness evolution raises the teacher's success from 33.4% to 63.6%; the final 4B student reaches 62.8%. Across four harness versions, distilled 4B students score close to their corresponding teachers, and later versions yield stronger students, showing that harness evolution gains carry into compact models. The harness gains also transfer to other frozen planners without retraining. On identical episodes, the final 4B student outperforms open 4B agents, the open 27B harness-RSI model SenseNova-RoboRSI, and our own teacher model placed in three competitors' harnesses. It stays close to its teacher on all three training benchmarks, and on three benchmarks never used for RSI or training it scores close to a 552B planner running the same harness. On the measured deployment episodes, it uses about one fifth of its teacher's accelerator time.

abstract.before: As publications and products on time series forecasting (TSF) proliferate, researchers face a growing burden of analyzing existing work. First, not all publications release code. For instance, only about 20% of arXiv TSF papers have a code link in the surveyed period. Second, released code also requires manual maintenance. Thus, TSF researchers must constantly adapt or implement existing works. However, independent implementations can differ in experimental settings and are difficult to maintain. We therefore propose to use AI agents for benchmarking TSF research and even supporting autoresearch, e.g., developing new TSF models. Yet directly applying existing coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, is suboptimal: prohibitive costs, limited scalability to large research projects (e.g., benchmarking), and lack of self-maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose TSFLab, a self-improving agent-agnostic"workbench"that equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost TSF research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Our experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking, and new method development. In reproduction and benchmarking, TSFLab improves task completion by 20-163% and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11-66% across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development also shows improved forecasting accuracy via TSFLab, with 32.8-73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2-68.8% less development time than the other settings.

abstract.before: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at this https URL .

abstract.before: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents. These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness. Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.

abstract.before: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

abstract.before: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p<1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.

abstract.before: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods'respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

abstract.before: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $\tau^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

abstract.before: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents'needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assistance when specific information needs arise. Upon an approved request, AOD retrieves relevant evidence from peer execution histories, selects a suitable peer, and generates a response tailored to the request. To determine when such assistance is worthwhile, we train a lightweight gate using paired team continuations, with supervision derived from final team outcomes and inference cost. Experiments on AppWorld and WebShop demonstrate that AOD consistently improves task performance over independent parallel execution while achieving lower inference cost than existing information-sharing baselines. These findings highlight the benefits of aligning peer communication with agents'evolving information needs to achieve more effective and efficient collaboration.
